::: {#sol-shape-rule}

A vector in $\reals^3$ is a $3 \times 1$ matrix,
so the same rule settles every case.

1.  $\matr{A}\matr{B}$: $(4 \times 3)(3 \times 2)$. The inner pair is $3$ and $3$, so it is
    defined, and the result is $4 \times 2$.
2.  $\matr{B}\matr{A}$: $(3 \times 2)(4 \times 3)$. The inner pair is $2$ and $4$, which do
    not match, so it is **not defined**.
    Matrix multiplication is not commutative, and this is the blunt form of
    that: swapping the order can leave an expression that means nothing.
3.  $\matr{A} \vx$: $(4 \times 3)(3 \times 1)$, defined, result $4 \times 1$ ---
    a vector in $\reals^4$.
4.  $\vx\' \vx$: $(1 \times 3)(3 \times 1)$, defined, result
    $1 \times 1$ --- a single number.
    The product is the inner product of @eq-inner-product.
5.  $\vx \vx\'$: $(3 \times 1)(1 \times 3)$, defined, result
    $3 \times 3$ --- a matrix.

The last two use the same two vectors and differ only in order,
and they return objects of different kinds.
Reading a transpose as decoration rather than as a shape change is the
commonest way to lose track of an expression.

:::
